drug_class: HER2-targeted antibody-drug conjugate (a type of targeted cancer therapy)
purpose: This medication is used to treat a certain type of breast cancer called HER2-positive breast cancer. It is typically given to adults who have already tried other treatments like trastuzumab (Herceptin) and a taxane chemotherapy. It can be used for early-stage or advanced breast cancer depending on your situation.
how_it_works: Think of this medicine as a smart missile — it has two parts working together. One part (trastuzumab, the antibody) seeks out and locks onto cancer cells that have a special protein called HER2 on their surface. Once it finds the cancer cell, it delivers the second part (emtansine, a powerful chemotherapy) directly inside the cancer cell to destroy it. This helps protect healthy cells from as much damage as a regular chemotherapy would cause.
common_side_effects: Fatigue (feeling very tired), nausea, headache, muscle or joint pain, low platelet counts (which can cause easy bruising or bleeding), elevated liver enzymes, constipation, and nosebleeds are among the most commonly reported side effects.
warnings: This medication can cause serious liver damage, so your doctor will monitor your liver with regular blood tests. It can also cause low platelet counts, which raises your risk of bleeding — let your doctor know right away if you notice unusual bruising or bleeding. It can harm an unborn baby, so do not become pregnant while on this medication and use effective birth control. In rare cases it can cause serious lung problems or heart problems, so report any new shortness of breath, chest pain, or swelling to your doctor immediately.
typical_dosing: This medication is given through an IV (intravenous infusion) directly into your vein at a clinic or infusion center. The usual dose is 3.6 mg per kilogram of your body weight, given once every 3 weeks. Your doctor or nurse will monitor you closely during and after the infusion, especially the first time.
